pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Cloud Types — identify cumulus (fluffy, fair-weather, low), stratus (flat grey layers, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (thin high wisps of ice) and know clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS1/KS2 weather observation and Y1 Seasonal changes (observe and describe weather); cloud identification is an observational science skill rather than a discrete statutory objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-ESS2-1 (describe typical weather) and K-ESS2-1 (observe/describe weather over time) as an observation-and-prediction skill. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach as a field-guide (name + look + altitude + weather it signals) PLUS the shared formation mechanism (vapour cools and condenses on tiny particles); use real sky photos/observation over the school week; connect cloud type to a simple forecast (cirrus → change coming; towering cumulus → showers).
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name and describe the three types from images; Tier B — explain clouds as condensed liquid droplets (not vapour) and predict weather from cloud type; Tier C — relate cloud height/type to air rising and cooling.
bestPractices: Use real sky photographs and regular outdoor observation — build a class cloud log over a week
Teach altitude as a defining feature (cirrus high and icy, cumulus/stratus lower) so height is part of identification
Explicitly state clouds are made of tiny LIQUID (or ice) droplets, not invisible vapour — confront the commonest cloud misconception head-on
Link each cloud type to a simple, testable weather prediction to give identification a purpose
If demonstrating cloud-in-a-jar, first show smoke dissipating alone so children don't mistake the smoke for the cloud
keyRepresentations: Altitude-layered sky diagram placing cirrus high, cumulus/stratus lower
Photo field-guide cards pairing each cloud with its name and typical weather
A cooling-air panel showing vapour condensing onto particles into droplets
A simple cloud → forecast lookup (fluffy = fair; grey layer = drizzle; high wisps = change coming)
commonMisconceptions: Clouds are made of water vapour or gas — visible clouds are tiny LIQUID (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible
Steam is water vapour — it is condensed liquid droplets too
In a cloud-in-a-jar demo, the smoke IS the cloud — the smoke provides particles for droplets to condense on
Clouds are solid/fluffy things you could stand on, rather than suspended droplets
All clouds mean rain — many (cumulus, cirrus) are fair-weather or high-and-dry

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners identify the three main cloud types — cumulus (fluffy, fair-weather, low), stratus (flat grey overcast layers that can bring drizzle) and cirrus (thin high icy wisps) — and learn that clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets (or, very high up where it is freezing, tiny ice crystals). Identification works best from real sky photos paired with altitude, and each type links to a simple, checkable weather prediction. The commonest misconception to confront directly is that a visible cloud is water vapour or gas; in fact vapour is invisible and the visible cloud is tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals.

activities.title: Altitude-layered sky field guide
feedback: If a learner sorts by shape alone, point to the height differences: cirrus high and icy, cumulus and stratus lower, so altitude is part of the identification.
If a learner says the cloud is vapour or gas, show the condensation close-up: vapour is invisible; what we see is tiny liquid droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when the air cooled.
When a forecast is revealed, prompt the learner to say why that cloud signals that weather, not just to read the label; treat the forecast as likely, then checked against the real sky.
activities.rationale: Identification by appearance and altitude is fundamentally a visual task, so a layered sky image where height is read at a glance makes the organising idea concrete. Linking each type to a forecast gives recognition a purpose, and a drill-down into condensation addresses the core misconception by showing it rather than only stating it.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.

A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Study one rich sky scene showing cirrus streaking high, cumulus billowing low, and a flat grey stratus sheet, and notice how the three types sit at different heights.

For each cloud, record its name, what it looks like, roughly how high it sits, and the weather it signals (cirrus: thin icy wisps, very high, a change may be coming; cumulus: fluffy, low, usually fair weather; stratus: flat grey layer, overcast, often bringing drizzle).
Reveal a 'What weather?' forecast for each cloud, then whenever you spot that cloud type in the real sky over the coming days, check whether the predicted weather follows.
Zoom into one cloud to see a model of invisible water vapour cooling and condensing onto tiny particles to form droplets, and state in your own words what the cloud is actually made of.
activities.intendedInsight: Clouds are not random blobs but a named, layered system you can read by look and height; and a visible cloud is made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals, not invisible vapour.

activities.title: Sort real sky photographs
feedback: If a learner mixes up stratus and cirrus, contrast a solid low grey sheet with thin high streaks and ask which sits higher.
If a learner expects rain from every cloud, point out that cumulus and cirrus are often fair-weather or high-and-dry; only some clouds (such as tall piled-up cumulus) signal showers soon.
activities.rationale: Practising with authentic images beyond idealised diagrams supports transfer to the real sky, and sorting with feedback turns passive recognition into active discrimination. The grouping-by-weather step also involves describing typical weather from observed data.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
NGSS 3-ESS2-1 frames describing typical weather conditions from observed data at grade 3.
learnerActions: Collect or view a set of real sky photographs and sort each one into cumulus, stratus or cirrus.
For each photo, name one feature that decided your choice (fluffy and piled, flat grey layer, or thin high wisps).
Group the sorted photos by the weather each type tends to bring and explain the pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: Real skies are messier than diagrams; applying the look-and-height features to genuine photos builds reliable recognition and connects type to likely weather.

activities.title: Cool-the-air cloud formation
feedback: If a learner thinks the cloud appears because vapour became visible, stress that vapour stays invisible and it is the new liquid droplets we can see.
If a learner imagines the cloud as a solid fluffy thing you could stand on, clarify that a cloud is countless tiny droplets suspended in the air, not a solid surface.

If demonstrating a cloud in a jar, first show smoke dissipating on its own so the learner does not mistake the smoke for the cloud — the particles only give the water vapour something to condense on to form droplets.
activities.rationale: A dynamic cooling demonstration makes the formation mechanism observable and ties the abstract word 'condense' to a visible change, directly targeting the vapour-versus-droplet misconception and the idea that a cloud is a solid object.
sourceClaims: A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Use a control that cools a pocket of air and watch invisible water vapour condense into a visible cloud of droplets as the temperature drops.
Describe the sequence: warm air holds invisible vapour, cooling makes the vapour condense onto tiny particles, and the gathered droplets become the cloud you can see.
Relate this to everyday examples such as breath fogging on a cold day or steam cooling above a kettle — both are condensed droplets, not vapour.
activities.intendedInsight: A cloud forms when cooling turns invisible water vapour into tiny liquid droplets that together become visible; the visible part is always liquid or ice, never the gas itself.

activities.title: Build a class cloud log
feedback: If a prediction fails, treat it as data: ask what else the sky showed and whether more than one cloud type was present.
Encourage noting altitude cues (very high wisps versus low fluffy heaps) to strengthen each day's identification.
activities.rationale: Regular outdoor observation over a week turns the field guide into a lived skill and connects naming to real weather outcomes, matching how weather observation is taught.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1 frames describing typical weather conditions from observed data at grade 3.
Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
learnerActions: Observe and photograph (or sketch) the sky at a set time across a week and name the cloud type each day.
Beside each entry, note the weather that followed and compare it with what that cloud type predicts.
At the end of the week, review which predictions held and discuss why a cloud type signals the weather it does.
activities.intendedInsight: Cloud identification is an observational skill: watching real skies over time links cloud type to weather and shows prediction can be tested.

activities.title: Check recognition and prediction
feedback: If a learner picks the high wisps as the rain sky, revisit that tall piled-up cumulus often signals showers soon, while high cirrus may signal a change later rather than immediate rain.
If a learner answers that a cloud is made of vapour, gas, smoke or cotton wool, correct it: a cloud is tiny liquid water droplets (sometimes ice crystals) formed when vapour cools and condenses.
activities.rationale: Matching and short questions give a clean check of identification and prediction, and including the ice discriminator and a 'what is it made of' item surfaces the key misconception.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.

A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Match each cloud image to its name (cumulus, stratus, cirrus).
Answer: which cloud is made mostly of ice crystals? (cirrus), and which sky — tall dark piled-up clouds or thin high wisps — is more likely to bring rain soon?
Explain in a sentence what a cloud is actually made of.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can name types from images, pick out the ice-cloud discriminator, and read cloud shape as a rain signal while stating the condensation model.

activities.title: Ask a weather watcher
feedback: Prompt the learner to connect the answer to a visible feature (height, shape, colour) so the reasoning stays grounded in observation.
If the conversation drifts to 'all clouds bring rain', redirect to naming a fair-weather cloud and its signal.
activities.rationale: Explanatory dialogue supports learners who reason by discussing, and it reinforces prediction; it works best alongside visual identification rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
learnerActions: Pose questions to a knowledgeable adult or imagined meteorologist, such as 'What does that cloud mean?' or 'Why do those two clouds bring different weather?'
Explain back, in your own words, the reasoning behind one answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through what a cloud signals deepens understanding of the type-to-weather link and invites reasoning, though the recognition itself still rests on seeing the clouds.

constraints: Identification is primarily a visual, height-based skill, so visual tasks should carry the core learning; discussion-only activities reinforce reasoning but do not by themselves replace seeing the clouds.

State explicitly that a visible cloud is tiny liquid droplets (or tiny ice crystals), not invisible water vapour, and not a solid thing you could stand on; this is the commonest misconception and must be confronted directly.

Not every cloud means rain — cumulus and cirrus are often fair-weather or high-and-dry; only relate specific types (e.g. tall piled-up cumulus) to imminent showers, and treat predictions as likely rather than certain.
Treat altitude as a defining identification feature (cirrus high and icy; cumulus and stratus lower), not just an extra fact.
A single sky image or diagram is a scaffold: pair it with real sky photos and outdoor observation so recognition transfers to genuine, variable skies.

In a cloud-in-a-jar demonstration, show smoke dissipating alone first so the smoke is not mistaken for the cloud; the particles only provide surfaces for water vapour to condense on, forming droplets.
A reveal-the-answer forecast should add new information a learner can check against the real sky, not merely restate the cloud's name.
Matching and short-question checks confirm recognition and prediction but do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation of cloud formation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three source claims (the misconception source and the Met Office/NOAA classification claim) are marked unverified in the original row; treat the cloud-type and misconception details as provisional pending source verification.

The original materials sometimes framed a static layered image as uniquely suited ('plays exactly to a static image's strength') and judged 3D as adding 'novelty more than insight' and a conversation as unable to deliver recognition 'as directly as a picture'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy findings; they are softened here to scoped suggestions. A fixed image cannot be manipulated but can still teach, and 3D or dialogue can support learning without being necessary.
Rain-signal guidance is simplified for ages 7–9: cloud appearance indicates likely rather than certain weather, so predictions should be treated as testable rather than definitive.

Ordinary cumulus is usually a fair-weather cloud, whereas tall, piled-up (towering) cumulus signals showers; the field guide labels cumulus 'usually fair weather' and the check specifies the tall form, so the two activities stay consistent for this age group.

The NGSS claim is attached to the photo-sorting and cloud-log activities only because their weather-grouping/observation steps involve describing weather from observed data; the discrimination/transfer rationale is otherwise supported by the cloud-type claim.

probeDeeper: Why can you see a cloud but not the water vapour rising off a wet playground?
The tall dark cloud and the thin wispy cloud are both 'clouds' — why do they bring such different weather?
When a cloud forms, what is happening to the water and where did it come from?
assess.correctAnswer: A cloud is made of tiny water droplets (and sometimes ice crystals) formed when water vapour cools and condenses. The tall, dark, piled-up cloud is far more likely to bring rain soon than the thin, high, wispy streaks.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Clouds are made of smoke / cotton wool / fog stuff'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link kettle-steam and breath-on-cold-glass to droplets condensing from vapour.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cloud is fluffy cotton-like stuff, not water.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Any cloud means rain is coming / all clouds are the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort cloud photos by the weather each type brings.
errorPatterns.distractor: Any cloud in the sky means it will rain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot tell rain clouds from fair-weather clouds

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A cloud is the water vapour itself — that's why we can see it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress vapour is invisible; the visible cloud is liquid droplets.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cloud is the water vapour, which is why we can see it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the visible cloud is vapour

responseLevels.gap: Describes clouds as smoke/cotton/gas; treats every cloud as the same.
responseLevels.full: Explains clouds as condensed water droplets and reads cloud type (tall/dark vs high/wispy) as a signal of likely weather, transferring to a new sky.
responseLevels.partial: Knows clouds are water droplets but cannot link cloud type to the weather it signals, or still confuses the visible cloud with invisible vapour.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: One day you see thick, tall clouds with dark bottoms piling up like cauliflowers. Another day, thin wispy streaks sit high in the sky. What is a cloud actually made of, and which sky is more likely to bring rain soon?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks clouds are smoke, gas or cotton-wool cannot connect a cloud to condensed water or read its shape as a rain signal; only the condensation model plus shape-reading answers both tiers.
